title: The DOM and CSSOM
summary: HTML and CSS parsing don't just produce text on screen — they build two live trees, the DOM and CSSOM, that everything from `getElementById` to layout reads from. Most rendering bugs trace back to a wrong mental model of one of these two.

slides.markdown:
"The DOM" gets used loosely to mean "the HTML," but they're not the same thing. The DOM is a **live, in-memory object tree** the browser builds by parsing your HTML — and once built, it can drift arbitrarily far from the original markup as JavaScript mutates it.

Alongside it sits a second tree most people forget exists as its own structure: the **CSSOM**, built from your stylesheets, encoding the cascade and specificity rules that decide which declaration wins for every element.

Both trees exist before a single pixel is painted, and the way they're built — streaming, incremental, occasionally blocked by a `<script>` tag — explains a long list of frontend behaviors: why `defer` matters, why mutating the DOM in a loop is slow, and why `document.querySelectorAll` results can silently go stale.

slides.sectionTitle: The DOM is a tree, not the HTML
slides.markdown:
The **Document Object Model** is a tree of objects in memory, each node exposing properties and methods — `.children`, `.appendChild()`, `.textContent`. Your original HTML is only the *initial instructions* for building it.

The distinction matters because the DOM is **live**: call `document.createElement()` and `appendChild()` from JavaScript, and the tree now contains a node that never appeared in the HTML source at all. View the page's "HTML" via browser DevTools (Elements panel) and you're looking at a **serialization of the current DOM**, not the original document — which is exactly why `view-source:` (raw HTML) and the Elements panel (live DOM) can show genuinely different content after JS has run.

Every DOM API call — `getElementById`, `classList.add`, `innerHTML =` — is reading or mutating this live tree, not editing a text file.

slides.subTitle: Tokenizing, then tree construction
slides.markdown:
HTML parsing runs in two coupled stages, per the WHATWG HTML spec's parsing algorithm:

1. **Tokenization** — the raw byte stream is chopped into tokens: start tags, end tags, text, comments.
2. **Tree construction** — tokens are consumed by a state machine that builds the DOM tree, following rules for implicit element insertion (yes, `<table><tr>` without a `<tbody>` still gets one inserted for you).

Both stages run **incrementally against a stream**, feeding tokens to tree construction as they're produced rather than waiting for the whole document — which is why the browser can start building (and rendering) a DOM before the HTTP response has finished arriving.

Unlike a JSON or XML parser, the HTML parser has **no syntax error state** — the spec defines exact recovery behavior for every malformed input, because the web had to keep rendering decades of broken markup. Concretely: an unclosed `

` auto-closes when a block element like `

` appears; a `` opened outside a `` but referenced inside one gets relocated by the "adoption agency algorithm"; stray closing tags with no matching open tag are simply ignored. None of this throws — it produces *some* DOM, deterministically, every time, even from garbage input. The consequence for you as an engineer: a browser rendering your markup "wrong" is never a parse error you can catch — it's the spec's recovery algorithm doing exactly what it's defined to do with your invalid nesting. The fix is validating your HTML structure yourself; the browser will never tell you it's broken.

slides.subTitle: Cascade, specificity, inheritance
slides.markdown:
CSS parsing produces its own tree — the **CSSOM** — where every node holds the fully **resolved** style for one selector's target, after three separate rules have been applied:

- **Cascade** — when multiple rules match the same element, origin and source order break ties (author styles beat user-agent defaults; later rules beat earlier ones at equal specificity).
- **Specificity** — a numeric weight per selector (ID beats class beats element) that overrides source order regardless of where a rule appears.
- **Inheritance** — some properties (`color`, `font-family`) flow down from ancestors by default; others (`margin`, `border`) do not, unless explicitly set to `inherit`.

Unlike the DOM, the CSSOM **cannot be built incrementally in the same streaming way** — a stylesheet's rules can be overridden by rules later in the same file, so the browser must have the complete, parsed stylesheet before it can resolve final values. That single fact is why CSS in the `<head>` is render-blocking by design, not by accident.

The DOM and CSSOM are built from different inputs, on different timelines, and are combined only later (in the render tree — covered in `critical-rendering-path`). Seeing them separately clarifies what each one actually owns.

The DOM answers "what elements exist and how do they nest." The CSSOM answers "for any given element, what's the final computed value of every style property." Neither tree knows about the other while it's being built.

slides.subTitle: Why scripts block parsing
slides.markdown:
A plain `<script src="...">` encountered mid-document **halts HTML parsing entirely** until the script downloads and finishes executing. This isn't an accident — it's a deliberate consequence of what scripts are allowed to do.

JavaScript can call `document.write()`, which injects new markup directly into the stream the parser is consuming, and it can query or mutate the DOM built so far via `document.querySelector`. The parser can't safely continue past the `<script>` tag without risking that the script changes the very tree it's building — so the browser plays it safe and blocks.

The preload scanner (covered in `url-to-page-lifecycle`) partly compensates by racing ahead to queue the script's *download*, but execution still blocks the main parser once the parser reaches that point in the stream.

slides.sectionTitle: defer vs async vs plain script
slides.markdown:
Three ways to include a script, three different parsing impacts:

| Attribute | Download | Execution | Parsing impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| (none) | blocks parser | immediately, blocks parser | HTML parsing fully halts until script runs |
| `async` | non-blocking, parallel | as soon as download finishes, whenever that is | parsing pauses briefly for execution, at an unpredictable point |
| `defer` | non-blocking, parallel | after parsing completes, in document order | parsing never pauses for it at all |

`async` scripts also run in **completion order, not document order** — if script B finishes downloading before script A, B executes first, regardless of markup order. That makes `async` a poor fit for scripts with dependencies between them; `defer` preserves order and is the safer default for most app code. `async` earns its keep for genuinely independent scripts like analytics, where execution order truly doesn't matter.

slides.sectionTitle: Live collections: the surprise in NodeList
slides.markdown:
`document.getElementsByClassName()` returns a **live** `HTMLCollection` — it re-evaluates automatically as the DOM changes, so removing matching elements while iterating over it can skip items, because the collection shrinks under you mid-loop.

`document.querySelectorAll()`, by contrast, returns a **static** `NodeList` — a snapshot at call time that doesn't update even if you later add or remove matching elements from the DOM.

This is a real, common source of "my loop skipped an element" bugs: swap `getElementsByClassName` for a loop that removes elements, and the live collection's shifting indices explain it immediately. Knowing which DOM APIs return live versus static collections is the difference between debugging this in seconds versus an hour.
